Dwelt
dwelt
v. (preterite of dwell: abode, resided; rendering Hebrew yashab and shakan, Greek skenoo and meno)
Preterite of dwell, from the Saxon dwellan, which first meant to delay or tarry and only later to reside — dwelling is tarrying that has become permanent. Hebrew shakan is to settle down, the root of mishkan, the tabernacle, and of the later term shekinah.

Biblical Definition

Dwelt is a quiet word carrying one of the highest doctrines in Scripture. John chooses it for the incarnation, and his Greek is precise: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The verb is skenoo, to pitch a tent, deliberately recalling the tabernacle in the wilderness where the glory settled between the cherubim; the eternal Word did not visit humanity but tented in it, and the glory once veiled behind curtains was now veiled in flesh. The Old Testament pattern behind this is the patriarchal life of faith, which Hebrews summarises: Abraham “sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob” (Hebrews 11:9) — men who owned the promise and pitched tents, because they looked for a city with foundations. Luke closes Acts with the same word used of unglamorous faithfulness: “And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him” (Acts 28:30), an apostle under guard, still preaching, the book ending without a verdict because the gospel's progress never depended on one.

Webster 1828 Definition

Preterite of dwell — abode, resided. John's word for the incarnation is skenoo, to pitch a tent: the Word was made flesh and tabernacled among us.

expand to see more

DWELT, pret. and pp. of dwell. [Sax. dwellan, to tarry.] Abode; resided; inhabited; continued in a place.

2. To remain; to continue; to be fixed in attention; as, to dwell upon a subject.

3. Of tent-dwelling; as, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, Heb. 11.

4. In Scripture, of the incarnation; the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, John 1.

5. Of the indwelling of God; as, in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily, Col. 2.

Key Scripture

John 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."

Hebrews 11:9 — "By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:"

Acts 28:30 — "And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him,"

Psalm 33:14 — "From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth."

Modern Corruption

The incarnation is often reduced to God visiting or appearing — a temporary manifestation. John's verb says the Word pitched his tent among us, took real flesh, and did not lay it down at the ascension.

expand to see more

Every ancient error about Christ's person can be described as a refusal of this verb. Docetism said he only seemed to have flesh; Apollinarianism gave him a body without a human mind; Nestorianism held the two natures so far apart that no single person truly dwelt among us; Eutychianism blended them into a third thing that is neither God nor man. Chalcedon answered them all with one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division, or separation — which is simply John 1:14 defended. The modern versions of the error are vaguer but the same: Christ as an inspired man, or as God appearing in human costume.

The principle to recover is the permanence of the dwelling. Christ did not shed his humanity when he ascended; he sits at the Father's right hand as the God-man and will return in the body in which he suffered. That is why Hebrews can make him a High Priest touched with the feeling of our infirmities, and why the patriarchs' tent-dwelling in Hebrews 11:9 is more than local colour — the men who dwelt in tents looked for a city, and the Word who tented among us is preparing it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yashab is to sit or remain, the ordinary word for residing, while shakan is to settle or tabernacle, giving mishkan and shekinah. Greek skenoo is to pitch a tent and meno is to abide or remain.

expand to see more

Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to sit, to remain, to inhabit; the common verb for dwelling in a place.

Hebrew shakan (H7931) — to settle down, to tabernacle; used of the glory dwelling between the cherubim.

Hebrew mishkan (H4908) — tabernacle, dwelling place; the tent God commanded Moses to raise.

Greek skenoo (G4637) — to pitch a tent, to tabernacle; John's verb for the incarnation.

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to remain; abide in me, and I in you.

Usage

"Of the incarnation: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us (John 1:14)."

"Of patriarchal faith holding the promise in tents: dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob (Hebrews 11:9)."

"Of unglamorous apostolic faithfulness: Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house (Acts 28:30)."
